heard: Black holes usually kill stars, but this one births them. Most supermassive black holes act as thermostats, heating gas to prevent star formation. But the Phoenix Cluster, discovered in 2010, is a rule-breaking monster in the southern sky. It generates more than 700 stars every year, shattering X-ray and star birth records. Our Milky Way forms only one or two stars in that same time. Chundra and Hubble found cavities and filaments, while Webb spotted the gas cooling between them. Despite weighing 10 billion suns, this black hole fails to heat nearby gas, allowing stars to form. This frantic growth spurt is unsustainable and will likely end within 100 million years. This makes the Phoenix cluster a rare exception, as black holes usually kill stars.
